triage.text: RT-PS-01 (party-slot concurrent-write race): DB unique constraint on (owner_identity, party_slot WHERE != PARTY_SLOT_NONE) — deferred pending SpacetimeDB partial-unique-constraint support.
triage.evidence: The premise is refuted by a LATER accepted decision. ADR-0106 D8 (docs/adr/0106-m15a-trading-spine.md:64): 'SpacetimeDB reducers execute in a single-threaded WASM environment. Read-check-write within one reducer is atomic with respect to all other reducers — no concurrent TOCTOU is possible.' That finding is now repo doctrine, cited at server-module/src/guards.rs:183, server-module/src/schema.rs:613, ADR-0131:100, ADR-0132:54, ADR-0170:58, ADR-0179:293. RT-PS-01's scenario ('two concurrent connections can each read occupied_slots before the other writes') is exactly the interleaving serialized execution forbids. The pinning test game-core/src/world.rs:1253 rt_ps_01_concurrent_slot_assignment_requires_db_uniqueness_constraint remains valid as a pure-layer soundness test, but its 40-line comment block (world.rs:1216-1237) is STALE PROSE asserting a race that cannot occur.

triage.evidence: The distinct error strings are still there, verbatim: server-module/src/trading.rs:305 `"counterparty has insufficient currency for this trade"` and trading.rs:357 `format!("counterparty has insufficient inventory for item {}", …)`. A ≤64-call binary search over offer amounts yields the counterparty's exact balance — an active oracle, strictly worse than the passive lower-bound leak the same ADR accepted. triage.text: (2) mutate-server lacks mutate-core's explicit [ ! -f missed.txt ] guard — but a missing file yields empty grep stdout and [ "" -gt … ] errors out under set -e, so this too fails loud, not vacuous-green.
triage.evidence: Closed, and the ADR's own reasoning was found WRONG in the process. justfile:131-134 now has the guard, with a comment recording the refutation: 'The explicit existence guard is NOT redundant with set -e (ADR-0183 D7, proved by execution): `|| true` swallows grep's exit 2, leaving missed="", and the resulting `[ "" -gt N ]` error is EXEMPTED from set -e because it sits in an if-condition — so without this guard the ratchet block is skipped and the gate exits 0 vacuously green.' A second belt was added at justfile:141-143.

triage.text: (3) wc -l (mutate-core) vs grep -c '' (mutate-server) count-idiom inconsistency is pre-existing and out of scope.
triage.evidence: Still divergent — and the divergence is now self-documented as a defect on the mutate-core side. justfile:85 `missed=$(wc -l < mutants.out/missed.txt)` (mutate-core, ZERO-TOLERANCE gate) vs justfile:138 `missed=$(grep -c '' mutants.out/missed.txt || true)` (mutate-server), whose adjacent comment (justfile:135-137) states the reason: 'grep -c "" counts lines regardless of a trailing newline (wc -l undercounts a newline-less last line)'. Consequence on the zero-tolerance gate: a missed.txt containing exactly one survivor with no trailing newline yields wc -l = 0 → VACUOUS GREEN on a real missed mutant. Narrow (cargo-mutants normally emits a trailing newline) but it is a silent-green class on the strictest gate in the repo, so severity MED not LOW. Aligns with post-mortem RF-1 (magnitude/edge collapsed at ingestion).
triage.suggested_slice: SL-J: normalise both mutation recipes onto grep -c '' with the existence guard + integer-shape belt already proven in mutate-server, and add a one-survivor-no-trailing-newline fixture tooth — touches: justfile, evals/mutate-core-recipe-integrity.eval.mjs, evals/nightly-smoke-wiring.eval.mjs

triage.text: D3 — 17.5e-2 decline-cooldown DEFERRED to M19 (decline-and-mute); record, don't build. HONEST SCOPE: the TTL bounds only the AFK/disconnected-challenger lockout; an ACTIVE attacker can re-challenge the instant its row is reaped/declined — the TTL does NOT bound that; recourse is the M19 decline-cooldown/mute primitive.
triage.evidence: Nothing shipped: `grep -rn 'cooldown|decline_cooldown|mute' server-module/src/pvp.rs` returns ZERO hits. The challenge lifecycle is unchanged (challenge_pvp at pvp.rs:871, decline at :1015-1035, reaper at :1221). So the harassment vector the ADR names honestly — an active attacker re-challenging immediately after every decline, with each Pending row locking BOTH parties out of new challenges via guards 5b/6 — is fully open. M19 is not in any spec or PLAN section I can find. Severity MED (not HIGH) because the exposure needs a motivated griefer and the victim can log out; it is a genuine denial-of-play surface, not a data or authz break.
triage.suggested_slice: SL-M: per-target decline cooldown — a private challenge_cooldown table keyed (challenger, target) written on decline/cancel, checked in challenge_pvp, reaped on TTL; pure is_cooldown_active in game_core::combat::pvp beside is_challenge_stale — touches: server-module/src/schema.rs, server-module/src/pvp.rs, server-module/src/pvp_tests.rs, game-core/src/combat/pvp.rs, evals/pvp-handshake-guards.eval.mjs

No re-arm branch (pathological-clock refire loop risk + YAGNI)'). Requires a backwards wall-clock step to trigger, has manual recourse, and the alternative was rejected on merit. triage.text: (c) The 'reaper fires' proof is static source-scan (EA-CHR-01..06, pvp-challenge-reaper eval) plus pure boundary tests — there is NO runtime firing test in this slice; PvP runtime coverage is slice 17.5f's charter.

So no scheduled reducer in the repo has a runtime firing test; all reaper evidence is static scan (evals/pvp-challenge-reaper.eval.mjs, EA-CHR-01..06 in pvp_tests.rs). Low severity: the static scans are thorough and the class is a known cost/benefit tradeoff, not an oversight.

triage.text: (d) Republish/restart survival of pending ScheduleAt::Time rows is not explicitly documented by SpacetimeDB 2.6 docs — schedule rows are durable table rows, so past-due fire-on-restart is expected but unverified; this applies equally to trade_offer_reaper.
triage.evidence: Genuinely unresolvable from the tree — it is an empirical question about SpacetimeDB 2.6.0 runtime behaviour, and the ADR is right that the docs do not state it. I did not run a live instance (READ-ONLY constraint) and static inspection cannot answer it. TO RESOLVE: publish to the isolated playtest DB (`just playtest-up`, MR_PLAYTEST_DB=monster-realm-playtest), create a Pending challenge, republish WITHOUT --delete-data, wait past CHALLENGE_TTL_MS (120s), and check whether the battle_challenge row is gone; repeat with --delete-data as the control. Worth folding into SL-Q rather than filing alone. Note it affects BOTH reapers and, if survival does not hold, every pending offer/challenge leaks across each republish — which for a solo local playtest with frequent wipes is currently invisible.

triage.text: (e) The trade-side schedule_trade_reaper deadline expression has the same scan-hole this slice's EA-CHR-06 closes for challenges (nothing pins its ms-floored math) — noted for the record, not fixed here.
triage.evidence: Confirmed unfixed. The challenge side HAS the tooth: server-module/src/pvp_tests.rs:2485-2530 EA-CHR-06 asserts the ms-floored deadline expression and the schedule insert ('EA-CHR-06 FAIL: the ms-floored deadline expression …'). The trade side does NOT: `grep -rn 'created_at_ms \* 1000|TRADE_OFFER_TTL_MS \* 1000' server-module/src/trading.rs server-module/src/trading_tests.rs evals/trade-reducer-security.eval.mjs` returns ZERO hits. The existing trade tooth (trading_tests.rs:1749-1824, EA-REAPER-01) pins only that schedule_trade_reaper is CALLED after the insert, not what deadline it computes. The consequence is exactly the failure ADR-0117 D4 designed against: if the deadline were computed from raw now-micros instead of the ms-floored created_at_ms, the one-shot could fire before is_offer_stale is true, no-op, and the offer would wedge both players' single trade slots forever — with no gate red.
triage.suggested_slice: SL-D: port EA-CHR-06 to the trade reaper — pin schedule_trade_reaper's ms-floored deadline expression (created_at_ms*1000 + TRADE_OFFER_TTL_MS*1000, saturating) and the schedule insert, with bad-fixture teeth for the raw-now-micros form — touches: server-module/src/trading_tests.rs, evals/trade-reducer-security.eval.mjs

triage.text: Accepted limitation 1 — Unbounded console.warn per unknown tag: each unknown-tag row issues one warn (no dedup); bounded by table size, not warn-once dedup (which would collide with the existing warn-assertion tests).
triage.evidence: Still undeduped: client/src/net/rowConvert.ts:85-88 `export function narrowTag<T extends string>(raw, known, enumName): T { if (!known.some((k) => k === raw)) { console.warn(…` with no seen-set. Real but small blast radius — it only triggers after a server adds an enum variant the client has not been regenerated for, and the eval (sdk-enum-exhaustiveness) is designed to red before that ships. The stated blocker (collision with warn-assertion tests) is solvable by injecting the dedup set. Note the interaction with ADR-0130: an unbounded warn stream does NOT reach the F9 bundle (the error ring is fed by reportError/window handlers, not console.warn), so there is no bundle-bloat risk.

triage.text: Accepted limitation 2 — Registry entries without narrowTag sites: e.g. ChallengeStatus feeds a bare-string store field; eval-only enforcement via C2/C3. Store-union changes out of scope.
triage.evidence: Explicitly accepted with the reason recorded in-code at client/src/net/rowConvert.ts:55-56 ('Registry entries WITHOUT a narrowTag call site feed bare-string store fields, where the eval alone forces author awareness (accepted limitation, ADR-0127)'). The eval-layer coverage (C2/C3 in sdk-enum-exhaustiveness.eval.mjs) is the deliberate enforcement tier. Narrowing every store field would be a large mechanical change with no measured defect behind it.

triage.text: Accepted limitation 3 — StatusEffect deliberately excluded: appears only on reducer args, never on row-read boundaries.
triage.evidence: A scoping decision with a stated structural justification (write-direction only, never read from a row by rowConvert — the same rationale that excludes PvpAction per ADR-0127 D2). Verified consistent: client/src/net/rowConvert.ts:59-68 HANDLED_ENUM_VARIANTS lists StatusKind (the row-read discriminant) but not StatusEffect. No work implied.

triage.text: Accepted limitation 4 — submitPvpAction unknown tag assumption: BSATN encode/server decode rejects it (SDK behavior, not client-verified).
triage.evidence: A documented reliance on platform behaviour on the WRITE direction, where the server is authoritative and rejects malformed input regardless. Verifying it client-side would test the SDK, not this codebase. Not schedulable.

triage.text: Accepted limitation 5 — PvP deadline-forfeit e2e deferred: 60s+ real wait; disconnect-forfeit path (pvp-full.spec.ts) covers the escrow semantics.
triage.evidence: Confirmed absent: `ls client/e2e/` shows pvp-full.spec.ts, pvp-side-b.spec.ts, pvp.spec.ts and ranked-forfeit.spec.ts but no deadline-forfeit spec, and pvp-full.spec.ts triggers forfeit by disconnect (ADR-0127 D3: 'immediate B disconnect (forfeit)'), never by the 60s PVP_TURN_DEADLINE_MS. So pvp_deadline_reaper's actual firing has zero runtime coverage — same class as ADR-0126 (c). The cost objection is real for a per-PR suite but not for a nightly job.
triage.suggested_slice: SL-Q (same slice as ADR-0126 (c)/(d) — one nightly scheduled-reducer firing test covering pvp_deadline_reaper, trade_offer_reaper and battle_challenge_reaper together)

triage.text: Accepted limitation 6 — --minify false caveat: a future CI step building a production bundle without minify would retain the hooks, but server authz still holds.
triage.evidence: Empirically refuted then superseded twice. ADR-0128 D3 measured it: 'vite build --minify false → also 0 window.__* bindings. The dead if (false) window assignments are eliminated by Rollup's DCE, which runs independent of minification … This refines ADR-0127's --minify false caveat (which implied the hooks are "retained"): the reachable binding is not retained; only dead object literals are.' ADR-0129 #4 then added scripts/verify-build-hooks.mjs, which scans the emitted dist for the window-BINDING fingerprints (not the bare token) precisely so an unminified build's dead literals do not false-positive while a real binding does.

triage.text: D3 — The remaining guard — a real vite build + grep of the artifact, which alone catches a committed --minify false — is deferred to pt-a2, alongside its mechanical release-verification.
triage.evidence: Discharged exactly as specified by ADR-0129 #4: scripts/verify-build-hooks.mjs scans client/dist/**/*.js for the .__game=/.__mrTrade=/.__mrPvp= binding fingerprints plus the Object.defineProperty escape, fails loud if dist is absent or empty, and is gated by evals/playtest-verify.eval.mjs on the pure checker (findDevHooks). ADR-0129's Context explicitly names the pt-a1 hand-off ('pt-a2 discharges exactly that'). The 2026-07-22 amendment (0129:120-147) later added bundleBakesDb to the same verifier. A model residual: it named the receiving slice, and that slice cited it back.

triage.evidence: An acknowledged tooling limitation with the compensating coverage already in place and documented: the 'unknown' path is covered via buildInfoFrom('unknown', …) at the formatter level plus the empirical build, and the ADR records that typeof on an undeclared global is safe in JS so the import cannot crash. The mitigation is already available (MR_BUILD_SHA env override, ADR-0128 D2). Listing it so it is not re-derived when a hosted milestone is scheduled; no slice now.

triage.text: F-7 — Build-time non-determinism in tests. Tests MUST assert via buildInfoFrom(sha, builtAt, isDev) with literal params (never import BUILD_INFO for a value assertion).
triage.evidence: A testing convention that is already enforced by the shape it prescribes — the ADR records that buildInfo.test.ts B1e/B1f pin the exact BuildInfo shape with toEqual, so a future added field (the leak vector via the ungated window.__mrBuild) fails those tests first. No deferred work; this is documentation of a rule in force.

triage.text: LOW-1 — Zero-width-char evasion of the DB guard. String.prototype.trim() does not strip U+200B/200C/200D/FEFF, so a VITE_STDB_DB of 'monster-realm' with a trailing zero-width space passes the dev-default guard. Fix, if ever needed: strip those characters before the guard, or reject non-ASCII DB names. Slated for pt-a2's mechanical release-verification if it lands a DB-name policy.
triage.evidence: pt-a2 did NOT land a DB-name policy (ADR-0129 records only a case-insensitive bash fold `${MR_PLAYTEST_DB,,}` for the recipe side, #2), so the slating expired unnoticed. Verified unfixed: `grep -n '200B|u200b|FEFF|zero-width|zeroWidth' client/src/net/connectionConfig.ts` returns ZERO hits. The ADR's own threat analysis remains correct — exploitable only if SpacetimeDB normalises the name AND an adversary controls the build env, and neither topology (local solo tester; hosted deploy pipeline) has an untrusted input path — so LOW is right. The fix is one normalisation line before the comparison.
triage.suggested_slice: SL-L: harden the prod DB guard — strip U+200B–U+200D/U+FEFF (or reject non-ASCII DB names) before the dev-default comparison, with fixtures for each zero-width form — touches: client/src/net/connectionConfig.ts, client/src/net/connectionConfig.test.ts

triage.text: LOW-2 — F-5 source-scan single-DEV-block assumption. The main.wiring.test.ts F-5 gate anchors on the FIRST if (import.meta.env.DEV); a future SECOND DEV block with an ungated hook between the two could evade the before-gate slice. Non-exploitable today (exactly one DEV block).

Measured: client/src/main.ts has 7 occurrences of `import.meta.env.DEV` (lines 183, 194, 222 as bare arguments; 1918/1920/1981 in comments; 2065 the one real gate block) — so exactly ONE `if (import.meta.env.DEV) {` statement remains, and the residual is still latent. Partial mitigation landed for a DIFFERENT defect in the same needle: client/src/main.wiring.test.ts:113 `const DEV_GATE_NEEDLE = '\nif (import.meta.env.DEV) {'` with the comment at :85-100 recording that ADR-0172 D7 fixed an earlier version where 'src.indexOf("if (import.meta.env.DEV)") resolved to that COMMENT, 147 lines above the real gate'. The first-block assumption itself was NOT addressed: F-5b/F-5c (:222/:251) still assert hook assignments appear AFTER gateIdx, so a hook placed between a first and a second DEV block would pass.
triage.suggested_slice: SL-L: make the F-5 gate count DEV gate blocks and assert each hook assignment lies inside a matched gate block (brace-depth walk), instead of a single before/after offset comparison — touches: client/src/main.wiring.test.ts

triage.text: Fingerprint residual (accepted, bounded): the fingerprint set matches the two shapes a real vite/terser build emits; alternate shapes (renamed-receiver defineProperty, space-after-comma, bracket assignment, globalThis[...], Reflect.set) are deliberately NOT matched.

The ADR also states the correct trigger ('If a future build-tool change makes any of these shapes reachable, extend the fingerprint set + add a tooth'). No work due.

triage.text: The 8 handler-wired / correlation-heavy variants (preRecruitHp, recruitAttempt, recruitResult, boxOpen, monsterRelease, reCatch, tradePropose, tradeConfirm) are defined-but-unemitted, parked to pt-b1b, which only adds eventRing.push(makeEvent…()) call sites + their delta-tracking + constructor tests.
triage.evidence: pt-b1b is an ORPHAN and all 8 sources are still dead. Constructors exist and are exported — client/src/ui/eventRing.ts:90 makePreRecruitHp, :94 makeRecruitAttempt, :98 makeRecruitResult, :102 makeBoxOpen, :106 makeMonsterRelease, :110 makeReCatch, :114 makeTradePropose, :118 makeTradeConfirm — but `grep -n 'eventRing.push' client/src/main.ts` returns only SIX sites, all from the pt-b1 core set: :815 zoneChange, :1742 battleStart, :1749 battleEnd, :1777 rankedMatch, :2578/:2624 connect, :2642 disconnect. `grep -rn pt-b1b docs/ client/src/` finds the string ONLY inside ADR-0130's own taxonomy table — no spec, no plan, no queue entry. CONSEQUENCE, which is why this is HIGH: ADR-0130's stated purpose is that 'the gate's H1/H2/H3 fun-hypotheses have no measurement'. H1 (recruit funnel) has 3 of 3 sources dead; H2 (box/release/re-catch) has 3 of 3 dead; H3 retains only rankedMatch, losing both trade sources. So the playtest gate the whole M-playtest arc exists to serve still cannot measure two of its three hypotheses, and the F9 bundle serialises 'whatever is in the ring' — i.e. a ring with no H1/H2 data. The work is also unusually cheap and pre-designed: the ADR specifies it as push call sites + delta tracking + constructor tests, with the ring API, overlay and bundle explicitly unchanged ('a clean YAGNI seam').
triage.suggested_slice: SL-E (= pt-b1b, as specified in ADR-0130 §2): wire the 8 parked event sources — recruit trio off the battle/recruit flow with the pre-attempt HP snapshot, box trio off boxView open + release + owned-species diffing, trade pair off the propose/confirm callbacks; seed every latch first-sight and reset all of them in resetPredictionState/onReconnect exactly as the pt-b1 latches do; keep payloads to numbers/ids/identity-hex so the T-BUNDLE-3 no-PII canary tooth still bites — touches: client/src/main.ts, client/src/ui/eventRing.ts, client/src/ui/eventRing.test.ts, client/src/main.wiring.test.ts

triage.text: Accepted residuals (no change): (a) lastOwnRating/activeBattleId also re-baseline on intra-session zone-switch, so a ranked/battle delta landing in the same batch as a zone transition is not emitted; (b) the ring snapshot() is an array-level defensive copy, deep-freezing is unwarranted YAGNI; (c) a battleEnd that resolves entirely during a disconnect gap is not observed.
triage.evidence: All three are explicitly accepted with reasoning, each traced to a named reviewer/red-team finding, and each is a deliberate consequence of the re-baselining posture the ADR adopts ('re-baselining is the ADR-accepted posture'). (a) and (c) are unlikely races whose alternative (straddling store.reset()) would double-count — strictly worse; (b) names YAGNI on data that is readonly-typed and read-only by every consumer. No implementable improvement is described.

triage.text: Alternatives considered — Add an evals/*.eval.mjs no-network gate. Deferred: would touch evals/** (out of touch-set); the source-scan tooth in main.wiring.test.ts covers it in-scope.

The in-scope substitute the ADR names does exist and is genuinely strong — the structural rule that client/src/ui/bugBundle.ts imports nothing from net/* makes the no-network property hold even against an indirect fetch in a helper (ADR-0130 §5, red-team H-2) — so the marginal value of a second layer is low. research.topic: Prior art for governing an autonomous, budget-constrained, long-running coding-agent loop: weekly-quota pacing, backlog integrity, instruction-surface accretion, orchestration-layer context management, and measuring whether a process change helped

findings.claim: The SRE multiwindow multi-burn-rate alert is the right SHAPE for the pacing gate, but only its structure transports — not its constants. The recommended table is Page/1h/5m/burn 14.4, Page/6h/30m/burn 6, Ticket/3d/6h/burn 1, with the short window set to ~1/12 of the long window. The long window establishes that meaningful budget was actually consumed; the short window confirms the condition is STILL TRUE at alert time and acts as an automatic reset valve so the alert stops within minutes of the condition clearing. Google names the drawback explicitly: 'complexity emerges from managing numerous parameters'.
findings.source: https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/ (SRE Workbook, 'Alerting on SLOs', multiwindow multi-burn-rate table)
findings.caveat: The 14.4/6/1 constants are calibrated to a 30-day error budget with three severity tiers and are meaningless transplanted to a 7-day credit allowance. What transports is (a) two windows, one for magnitude and one for currency, and (b) THE SHORT WINDOW AS A RESET PREDICATE. That second property is the direct fix for the 83.9h stranded done-event and the ~21h of self-disable: this loop has trip conditions with NO reset predicate at all. Every state a tick can enter must carry the condition that exits it.

findings.claim: Error budgets are designed to be SPENT, and 100% is explicitly the wrong target: 'if the team is having trouble launching new features, they may elect to loosen the SLO (thus increasing the error budget)'. Unused budget is treated as evidence of excessive conservatism, not as a win.
findings.source: https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/ (SRE Book, 'Embracing Risk')
findings.caveat: This is the single most important framing correction, and it INVERTS the usual burn-rate alarm. The operator's constraint is 'idle hours are free; optimise value per weekly credit'. Therefore ending a week at 60% utilization is a FAILURE of the same kind as hitting overage — allowance was forfeited. The pacing instrument must be TWO-SIDED: a floor ('behind pace, start work') as well as a ceiling. A one-sided ceiling alarm will silently push the loop toward chronic underspend, which is the failure mode a naive reading of burn-rate alerting produces here.

findings.claim: Google's error-budget policy on exhaustion is a change freeze with a named exemption list: 'all changes and releases other than P0 issues or security fixes will be halted until the service is back within its SLO'. The policy text states the freeze 'is not intended as punishment' but as a forced reprioritisation, and escalation is to a named human (the CTO) when the calculation is disputed.
findings.source: https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/
findings.caveat: Two transportable properties: (1) the freeze has a WRITTEN EXEMPTION CLASS (security), which is exactly what the 6 blind security evals / 14r-c-2 would need to remain launchable under a pacing hold; (2) the dispute path terminates at a human, not at the automation. Do NOT transport the freeze semantics themselves — a freeze at exhaustion is the kill-switch shape already refuted (DO-NOT-RETRY #1).

findings.claim: Cloud budget systems are documented as ALERT-ONLY by default and explicitly disclaim capping: 'Setting an alerts-only budget doesn't automatically cap Google Cloud or Google Maps Platform usage or spending... they don't automatically prevent the use or billing of your services'. Budgets separately support ACTUAL-cost thresholds and FORECAST-cost thresholds (forecast projects cost to the end of the calendar budget period).
findings.source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets
findings.caveat: The actual-vs-forecast split is the missing distinction in this loop. The governor currently reasons only about a level. With a monotone weekly gauge and a known reset time, a forecast threshold ('projected end-of-week utilization > 100%') is computable from two samples and fires DAYS before an actual-level threshold — which is what would have flagged the 29->90% week on roughly 08-08 rather than at 0.90 on 08-10. Note the ecosystem-wide lesson: the mature, widely-deployed systems chose alerting over capping.

findings.claim: AWS Budgets Actions is the closest production analogue to the operator's D4 ('cap = decomposition target at planning time, headroom query at run time'). Actions are configured to run 'either automatically or after your manual approval', and the canonical action is a DENY-NEW policy, not a terminate: 'You can use SCPs so that you don't need to provision any new resources during the budget period.' A separate documented step exists for 'Reviewing and approving your budget action'.
findings.source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/budgets-controls.html
findings.caveat: This is prior art for the exact three-way split the operator wants: threshold -> deny NEW provisioning (start nothing new), leave RUNNING resources alone (finish in-flight), and route the ambiguous case through an approval gate rather than an automatic action. It is also prior art that a cap-breach can legitimately be a QUERY: the approval workflow exists precisely because automatic enforcement was judged too blunt for the ambiguous cases.

findings.claim: 'Admit no new work, do not disturb work in flight' is a named, independently reinvented primitive in at least three production systems: kubectl cordon ('Mark node as unschedulable') which prevents new scheduling but does NOT evict running pods — explicitly distinct from kubectl drain which evicts; and Jenkins quietDown ('puts Jenkins in a Quiet mode, in preparation for a restart. In that mode, Jenkins doesn't start any build') with running jobs allowed to complete and new triggers QUEUED rather than dropped, plus an explicit cancelQuietDown to disarm and a timeout thread that reverts to normal.
findings.source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_cordon/ ; Jenkins CLI quietDown/cancelQuietDown/safeRestart/safeExit (docs.cloudbees.com/d/kb-203737684 and the jenkins.io CLI reference)
findings.caveat: D1 is not a bespoke policy; it is cordon. Three further properties of these systems are the direct fix for the two-actor kill-switch: (1) the pause state is a DIFFERENT state from shutdown (cordon != drain; quietDown != safeExit) — so a self-armed pace hold must not be the same flag as an operator stop; (2) the pause has an explicit disarm command distinct from arming; (3) Jenkins' quiet mode AUTO-EXPIRES on a timeout. The Jenkins auto-expiry and queue-don't-drop details are REPORTED from secondary/KB sources, not fetched from jenkins.io primary docs — verify before implementing. Critically: cordon does NOT sit above the event queue. Queued items are still accepted and processed when the state clears; only ADMISSION is blocked. The 83.9h stranded done-event is a defect of flag PLACEMENT, and cordon shows the correct placement.

findings.claim: Google's static-analysis programme sets a hard precision floor for anything surfaced in-workflow: 'Produce less than 10% effective false positives' (their overall measured rate is 'just below 5%'), the FP rate is CONTINUOUSLY MONITORED via a 'NOT USEFUL' button, and 'User trust is extremely important for the success of static analysis tools.' Their earlier standalone-dashboard approach with per-user customisation FAILED — it 'resulted in hidden bugs and suppressing feedback' — and was replaced by surfacing findings at the code-review point where 'developers are already in a change mindset'.
findings.source: https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch20.html (Software Engineering at Google, ch.20 'Static Analysis'); Sadowski et al., 'Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google', CACM 61(4), doi 10.1145/3188720
findings.caveat: gating_test_audit at 0 true positives in 11 in-window flags and 0 across all 446 v3-era rows is a 100% effective-FP rate — an order of magnitude past the documented abandonment threshold. Google's evidence says the correct action is removal or demotion to audit-only, not tuning. The same source also condemns the current prompt architecture by analogy: an always-resent doctrine file is the standalone dashboard — universally visible, actionable at no particular decision point. Their measured answer was to move the rule to where the change is being made. In this loop that is the per-slice brief (which measurably works: 0 of 18 merges re-derived scope) or a gate.

findings.claim: Google's Python and Java style guides require a TODO to carry a link to a TRACKED artifact, and state the reason: 'A bug reference is preferable because bugs are tracked and have follow-up comments.' The older TODO(username) form is explicitly 'discouraged for use in new code'. The in-file tag is a POINTER to the queue; it is never the record itself.
findings.source: https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html (TODO Comments); https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html
findings.caveat: This is the precise diagnosis of RF-3. The ADR Residuals section is a TODO(username)-shaped record: it names the work but points at nothing tracked, so nothing accrues follow-up state and nothing can close it. The measured consequence — 13.1-day mean latency, 14r-c-2 (6 blind security evals) existing on disk nowhere but the post-mortem — is the exact failure the Google guides changed their rule to prevent. The migration is: every residual line must carry an ID that resolves in a registry, and the ADR prose becomes a pointer, not a store.

findings.claim: PEP 350 (Codetags) — the most serious attempt to standardise structured in-file work tags (TODO/FIXME/BUG/RFE with fields for initials, date, priority and tracker ID) — is officially REJECTED: 'While the community may be interested, there is no desire to make the standard library conform to this standard.' Its envisioned tooling (roadmap generators, lint validators, a story-management system needing no separate tracker) was never built at scale.
findings.source: https://peps.python.org/pep-0350/
findings.caveat: Honest negative result, and it cuts against the obvious fix. Do NOT design a rich in-file residual grammar and hope tooling follows — that is the documented dead end. The pattern that DID survive is the minimal one: a tag carrying nothing but a tracker ID (finding above). Corollary for this project: the residual row's in-ADR form should be as close to a bare ID plus one line as possible, with all structure living in the registry the generator emits.

findings.claim: THE QUEUE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS REPO AND IS ALREADY IN CI. scripts/adr-digest.mjs (871 lines) parses every ADR, has generic header-field extractors (extractBoldField at :123, extractListField at :136), a per-ADR validator (validateAdr at :242), a cross-ADR relational validator (validateBacklinks at :509), and a --check mode wired into CI via justfile:238-240 and evals/adr-digest.eval.mjs. It already enforces a controlled vocabulary (SUBSYSTEM_VOCAB at :22).
findings.source: /home/mdrewt/projects/ai-apps/claude-harness/projects/monster-realm/scripts/adr-digest.mjs:22,123,136,242,509; justfile:232-240; evals/adr-digest.eval.mjs
findings.caveat: This reframes A11 from 'build a residual registry' to 'add one list field to a parser that already runs on every ADR in CI'. Contrast with the current state, measured: residual headings are free-form prose in at least four mutually incompatible shapes — '## Residuals' (0081:74, 0095:94, 0122:141), '## Residuals / follow-ups' (0192:108), '## Residuals (recorded for the supervisor)' (0170:265), '### Residual — <sentence>' (0181:158, 0181:193). Nothing can parse that set, which is why 21 Residuals sections have zero mechanical consumers. The cheapest correct change is a header field, e.g. '- Residuals: R-0193-1, R-0193-2', extracted by the EXISTING extractListField.

findings.claim: THE RATCHET PATTERN IS ALSO ALREADY IMPLEMENTED HERE, correctly, and should be copied rather than redesigned. adr-digest.mjs uses an era cutoff (BACKLINK_ERA_MIN = '0151', :57) so the gate binds only on new work; a grandfather set KNOWN_BACKLINK_GAPS (:75-81) documented as 'THIS SET MAY ONLY SHRINK'; a frozen duplicate of the set in evals/adr-backlink-corpus.eval.mjs asserting set EQUALITY 'so growth needs two visible edits in two directories'; a key-format validator (:83-93) that exits 2 on a malformed key because 'a typo'd key is inert: it tolerates nothing and the ratchet can never retire it'; and an error when a grandfathered gap is already fixed 'so the set cannot silently rot'. This independently reproduces Google's documented policy: 'we generally focus on newly introduced warnings; existing issues in otherwise working code are typically only worth highlighting... if they are particularly important.'
findings.source: /home/mdrewt/projects/ai-apps/claude-harness/projects/monster-realm/scripts/adr-digest.mjs:55-96; https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch20.html
findings.caveat: This is a stronger local template than ADR-0011 for anything with a legacy corpus, and it is the correct answer to DO-NOT-RETRY #4 (mutation survivors): a monotone-shrinking exemption set with a rot detector, not an absolute cap. Reuse it verbatim for the residual registry — a RESIDUAL_ERA_MIN plus a frozen set of the 75 pre-existing Residuals sections that may only shrink. That converts a 367-item backlog from a blocking migration into a background ratchet.

findings.claim: Google's monorepo practice validates the touches: discipline and locates the defect in the sink, not the rule: a CL should be 'one self-contained change', 'The CL makes a minimal change that addresses just one thing', and 'It's usually best to do refactorings in a separate CL from feature changes or bug fixes' — with a narrow carve-out: 'Small cleanups such as fixing a local variable name can be included inside of a feature change or bug fix CL.' The reviewer standard separately instructs approval 'once it is in a state where it definitely improves the overall code health... even if the CL isn't perfect' and that reviewers 'should not require the author to polish every tiny piece of a CL'.
findings.source: https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html ; https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html
findings.caveat: Confirms RF-3's framing: the prohibition is right, the missing piece is where the deferred item goes. Note also that Google's carve-out for in-scope cleanup is deliberately tiny (a local variable name) — which sizes the bounded boyscout allowance far smaller than the term usually implies.

findings.claim: A bounded boyscout allowance is a COMPLEMENT to a queue and cannot substitute for one — and the boyscout-rule literature is folklore, not evidence. The published material is opinion blogging on both sides (scope-creep and review-size objections; Fowler's opportunistic-refactoring taxonomy of litter-pickup / easier-to-add-a-feature / easier-to-understand). No controlled study of efficacy or harm was located.
findings.source: martinfowler.com/bliki/OpportunisticRefactoring.html and the surrounding blog literature; NO primary/empirical source located
findings.caveat: Mark as FASHIONABLE BUT UNEVIDENCED. Two project-specific reasons it must stay tiny here, both measured, both stronger than the generic argument: (1) it directly attacks the property that makes fan-out safe — C6 already records 3 of ~20 merges hitting sibling/doc conflicts on DECLARED touches alone, so widening the effective touch set raises collision probability on the mechanism (mr-disjoint) that is already comparing too narrow a set (A6); (2) it cannot possibly absorb the items that actually got lost — 6 blind security evals is a slice, not litter. Size the allowance at Google's carve-out (rename-scale, same file, zero new symbols) and route everything else to the registry.

findings.claim: The proven rollout sequence for a new gate is audit-first, enforce-later, with the audit output as the precision baseline. OPA Gatekeeper ships three enforcementActions — deny (default), dryrun ('allows constraints to be tested in a running cluster without enforcing them. Cluster resources that are impacted by the dry run constraint are surfaced as violations in the status field'), and warn (dryrun plus immediate feedback on why it would have been denied) — with the documented recommendation 'When rolling out new constraints to running clusters, the dry run functionality can be helpful.' Kyverno's validationFailureAction: Audit|Enforce is the same pattern.
findings.source: https://open-policy-agent.github.io/gatekeeper/website/docs/violations/
findings.caveat: Combined with the <10% effective-FP floor, this is a complete, evidenced recipe that would have prevented gating_test_audit: ship every new gate in dryrun, record every would-have-fired event with its adjudication, and promote to enforce ONLY after the measured effective-FP rate clears the floor over a stated number of firings. It also yields the pre-period of a pre/post evaluation for free, which is exactly the measurement debt in finding 17. Apply this to the pacing gate itself: run the utilization band in dryrun for at least one full reset cycle before it can hold a launch.

findings.claim: For orchestration-layer context management the published techniques are compaction (summarise and reinitiate a fresh window, 'starting with maximum recall, then improving precision'), structured note-taking to an external file pulled back in later, sub-agent architectures where each sub-agent has a clean window and returns 'a condensed, distilled summary of its work (often 1,000-2,000 tokens)', and just-in-time retrieval via 'lightweight identifiers (file paths, stored queries, web links)' loaded at runtime instead of pre-loading.
findings.source: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents
findings.caveat: VENDOR SOURCE, AND EXPLICITLY UNEVIDENCED. The article presents no controlled data, no improvement percentages, and no benchmark for any of the four techniques; the 'context rot' and 'attention budget' claims cite needle-in-a-haystack results and human working-memory analogies. Treat the techniques as engineering conventions to be locally A/B'd, not as established results. All four are reachable from the CLI without the API beta flags.

findings.claim: There is a serious published counter-argument to parallel sub-agents: 'Share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages' and 'Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results' — the failure mode being parallel sub-agents making mutually incompatible implicit choices that the coordinator cannot reconcile. The recommended default is a single-threaded linear agent, adding an intermediate compressing model only when the window would overflow. The author concedes the piece is 'based on internal observations' and 'our theories are likely not perfect'.
findings.source: https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents
findings.caveat: REASONING ONLY, no data — but it reconciles cleanly with the local measurements and sharpens the post-mortem's own conclusion. The reviewer/red-team sub-agents are ADVISORY: they return findings and make no implementation decisions, so they are outside the failure mode described and their measured value (93 runs, ~$171/wk, a merge-blocker found before code existed) stands. The tester role — 46% of subagent spend, median 58 turns, and the role that WRITES — is the one carrying the conflicting-implicit-decisions risk. This is an independent argument for the post-mortem's 'protect reviewer/red-team, target tester' conclusion, arrived at from a different direction.

findings.claim: Pre-registration is the established remedy for exactly this project's measurement failure: specifying hypotheses, design and analysis plan in a registry BEFORE data collection, whose primary value is 'constraining researchers' degrees of freedom' and separating confirmatory from exploratory claims (guarding against HARKing — hypothesising after results are known).
findings.source: Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven & Mellor, 'The preregistration revolution', PNAS 115(11):2600-2606, 2018, https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1708274114
findings.caveat: The specific local defect — 'the largest intervention replaced its own instrument in the same commit' — is the software analogue of changing the outcome measure after seeing the data. Pre-registration forbids it structurally. The minimum viable form here needs no new infrastructure: before a loop-infra change lands, write into the ADR header the named counter, its CURRENT measured value, the predicted post-change value, the holding period, and the REFUTED condition. That is ADR-0011's shape (named counter, measured defect, post-fix count of zero holding 14 days) made mandatory and, crucially, written BEFORE rather than after.

findings.claim: Multi-metric frameworks exist specifically because single metrics are gameable. SPACE (Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication, Efficiency) states productivity 'cannot be reduced to a single dimension or metric' and recommends selecting metrics that are in tension so one cannot be improved without visibly worsening another. DORA's four keys are two throughput and two stability measures for the same reason, and DORA's own guidance is that they are system- and team-level and must not be applied to individuals, because that 'incentivizes gaming, inflated commit volume, artificially split batches'.
findings.source: Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Houck, Butler, 'The SPACE of Developer Productivity', ACM Queue 19(1), doi 10.1145/3454122.3454124; https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/devops-sre/using-the-four-keys-to-measure-your-devops-performance
findings.caveat: The 'metrics in tension' formulation is widely repeated in secondary sources; the primary papers state the multi-dimension requirement and the anti-gaming rationale, and the exact tension phrasing should be attributed as convention rather than quoted as a finding. The applicable consequence is concrete: this project's output-volume channel is ALREADY saturated (82,076 insertions, 16.7% production source, 173 total production-source deletions), so any metric that improves when the loop emits more lines is dead on arrival — which independently confirms DO-NOT-RETRY #10 and #11.

findings.claim: The seven_day utilization gauge is a CUMULATIVE MONOTONE NON-DECREASING signal within a reset window, which makes it recoverable despite being sparsely sampled, quantized, lagging and absent on rejected events. The measured sequence 29 -> 33 -> 52 -> 59 -> 74 -> 83 -> 85 -> 87 -> 90 across Thu 08-06 20:00 -> 08-10 05:08 is strictly non-decreasing.
findings.source: Orchestrator-supplied measured telemetry sequence; rate_limit_info objects in stream-json logs; anchor $MEM/.weekly-reset-anchor (1784851200)
findings.caveat: INFERRED from the observed sequence plus the semantics of a cumulative fraction — not proven from vendor documentation, and worth one explicit check. If it holds, three useful properties follow with no new infrastructure: (1) max() over the window is a valid LOWER BOUND, so no interpolation or decay model is needed; (2) a 'rejected' event, which carries no utilization, can be recorded as 1.0 without loss — the binary and the gauge stop being in conflict, which is the whole of RF-1 for this signal; (3) two timestamped samples plus the known Thursday 20:00 reset give a forecast-to-budget ratio directly, enabling the forecast-threshold pattern from finding 4.

findings.claim: The harness's SHARE of account utilization is measurable from data the loop can already collect, and is currently the binding unknown behind every 'this returns N percentage points' estimate. Paired observations of (delta local ledger cost) against (delta seven_day utilization) over intervals when a harness session is the only active consumer yield a share coefficient; the internal governor's measured 1.39x under-report (64.7% reported vs 90% actual) is one such paired observation and is itself evidence that a substantial fraction of the account gauge is NOT harness spend.
findings.source: Orchestrator-supplied measured values (64.7% governor vs 90% account, week of 2026-08-06); mr-native-tick.sh:364; mr-supervisor-prompt-native.md:116
findings.caveat: INFERRED. This is the correct thing to measure FIRST, because without it the pacing gate cannot distinguish 'the loop is burning too fast' from 'the operator used Claude heavily on another machine today' — and those two states demand opposite responses (slow the loop vs. the loop is not the problem and slowing it forfeits allowance for nothing). D2 makes the account gauge the SSOT for the DECISION, but the local ledger remains necessary as the ATTRIBUTION signal. Do not delete it.

research.recommendation:
WHAT TO DO

1) Pacing: build a CORDON, not a governor. The evidenced primitive is admission control — kubectl cordon ("mark unschedulable", running pods untouched), Jenkins quietDown ("doesn't start any build", running jobs complete, new triggers QUEUED not dropped), AWS Budgets' deny-new-provisioning SCP. D1 is already this pattern; implement it as such and inherit its four properties: (a) the pause state is DISTINCT from the stop state (cordon != drain; quietDown != safeExit) — this splits the two-actor kill switch by construction: a self-armed pace hold and an operator stop become different files with different disarm paths; (b) the hold sits BELOW the event queue, blocking only admission of new slices, so a finished slice's done-event is always harvested (directly fixes the 83.9h strand); (c) the hold AUTO-EXPIRES on a timeout unless re-armed, so no state can persist past its cause; (d) arming and disarming are separate named commands.

2) Make the gauge two-sided and forecast-based. Persist every rate_limit_info object whole — never the status bit alone (mr-native-tick.sh:364; add `utilization` to the field list at mr-supervisor-prompt-native.md:116). Exploit monotonicity: max() over the window is a valid lower bound, and a `rejected` event records as 1.0. Then run a FORECAST threshold (projected end-of-week utilization at current pace vs. 100%, against the verified Thursday 20:00 anchor) rather than a level threshold — that fires days earlier, which is the whole point. Bands: below-pace -> START WORK (underspend is a real failure; SRE's "100% is never the right target" argument inverts here because idle credits are forfeited, not saved); on-pace -> normal; forecast-breach -> prefer smaller slices and defer large ones (D3: defer, never demote); near-ceiling -> cordon. Borrow the SHORT-WINDOW-AS-RESET trick from the multi-burn-rate table, not its 14.4/6/1 constants: every band must carry the predicate that exits it.

3) Measure the harness's SHARE before tuning anything. Log paired (delta local cost, delta account utilization) observations. Without this the gate cannot tell "the loop is burning too fast" from "the operator used Claude elsewhere today", and those demand opposite responses. Keep the local ledger — D2 correctly makes the account gauge the SSOT for the DECISION, but the ledger is the only possible ATTRIBUTION signal.

4) Backlog: add ONE list field to a parser that already runs in CI. Do not build a registry. scripts/adr-digest.mjs already has extractListField (:136), validateAdr (:242), validateBacklinks (:509), a controlled vocabulary (:22) and a --check gate (justfile:238-240, evals/adr-digest.eval.mjs). Add a header field `- Residuals: R-0193-1, ...`, have the generator emit the rows into a JSON artifact, and adopt Google's TODO rule exactly: the ADR prose becomes a POINTER carrying a tracked ID, never the record ("a bug reference is preferable because bugs are tracked and have follow-up comments"). PEP 350's rejection is the warning: keep the in-file grammar minimal, put all structure in the generated artifact.

5) Ratchet the 367-item legacy backlog; do not migrate it. Copy the pattern already working at adr-digest.mjs:55-96 verbatim — an era cutoff (RESIDUAL_ERA_MIN), a grandfather set that MAY ONLY SHRINK, a frozen duplicate in an eval asserting set equality so growth needs two visible edits, a malformed-key validator (an inert exemption is worse than none), and a rot detector that errors when a grandfathered item is already fixed. This is also the correct answer to the mutation-survivor cap (DO-NOT-RETRY #4).

6) Ship every new gate in DRYRUN first (Gatekeeper enforcementAction: dryrun -> warn -> deny). Promote to enforcing only after the measured effective-false-positive rate clears Google's <10% floor over a stated number of firings. Apply this to the pacing gate itself: one full reset cycle in dryrun before it may hold a launch. This also yields the pre-period of a pre/post evaluation for free.

7) Retire gating_test_audit rather than tune it. 0 true positives in 11 in-window flags and 0 across 446 v3-era rows is a 100% effective-FP rate — an order of magnitude past the documented abandonment threshold, and Google's measured lesson is that trust, once lost, is not recovered by tuning. Keep mr-audit:22-38.

8) Instruction surface: the argument is placement, not size. An always-resent doctrine file IS the standalone warnings dashboard that Google measured and abandoned — visible to everyone, actionable at no decision point. Move each normative rule to where the decision is made: the per-slice brief (measurably works — 0 of 18 merges re-derived scope) or an executable gate. Adopt the test "every normative rule must name either a mechanical consumer or an owning gate; a rule with neither is deleted or converted." That test would have caught `touches:`, `after:` and the 21 Residuals sections years ago. DO NOT SHORTEN THE BRIEF; anything added there is multiplied by ~500 turns, so additions must be single lines.

9) Context: take the two changes with local evidence, defer the rest. (a) Route orchestrator navigation through the retrieval index its own sub-agents already use — Bash 2,135 / Grep 0 / Glob 0 / codegraph_explore 0 against 47 sub-agent calls is a measured navigation defect, and it is one line in the brief. (b) Place segment boundaries at COMPLETED SUB-GOALS with a written handoff (the monster-realm-*-progress.md artifact already exists), never at a fixed turn count — relaunch re-pays the preamble plus 23.9%-of-volume re-orientation, so an eager turn cap can cost more than it saves. Treat compaction, note-taking and JIT retrieval as conventions to be locally A/B'd, not as results: the vendor source offers zero controlled data for any of them.

10) Measurement: pre-register, and never change instrument and treatment in one commit. Before a loop-infra change lands, write into its ADR header the named counter, its current MEASURED value, the predicted post value, the holding period, and the REFUTED condition. Pick metrics in tension (SPACE/DORA), and reject any metric that improves when the loop emits more lines — the output channel is already saturated (16.7% production source, 173 production deletions). The least gameable candidate available here is REDISCOVERY COUNT: defects found by a more expensive detector than the one that should have caught them. It cannot be lowered by producing more output, and it is exactly what 14r-c-2, ADR-0165 and the 6 blind security evals all are.

WHAT NOT TO DO

- Do not build a burn-rate ALARM (one-sided ceiling). It will drive chronic underspend, which under this operator's economics is the same failure as overage. The gauge must have a floor.
- Do not transport the SRE burn-rate constants (14.4 / 6 / 1). They are calibrated to a 30-day error budget. Only the two-window shape and the reset predicate transport.
- Do not implement the error-budget FREEZE. Freeze-at-exhaustion is the kill-switch shape already refuted; cordon is the correct primitive. Do borrow the freeze's written SECURITY EXEMPTION so 14r-c-2-class work stays launchable under a hold.
- Do not design a rich in-file residual grammar and expect tooling to follow. That is PEP 350, and it was rejected.
- Do not migrate the 367 legacy residuals as a blocking change. Ratchet them.
- Do not rely on a bounded boyscout allowance as the sink. The literature is folklore with no controlled evidence either way, and here it actively attacks the touches: disjointness that makes fan-out safe (C6 already shows 3 of ~20 merges conflicting on declared touches alone). Size it at Google's carve-out — rename-scale, same file, no new symbols — and route everything else to the registry.
- Do not tune gating_test_audit, do not enforce any new gate before its dryrun period, and do not add an ADR defer-phrase denylist as a blocking gate (already refuted).
- Do not justify any prompt change on token cost (~$83/yr, 0.087%), and do not adopt a numeric line ceiling as the mechanism — no evidence supports a specific number; the evidenced criterion is "does this rule have a consumer".
- Do not run the fable-vs-opus A/B, or any process A/B, until step 10's instruments exist and have a baseline. Every quality column is currently dead; an A/B on dead instruments yields a clean cost signal, a null quality signal, and the predictable wrong conclusion.
unknowns: Whether seven_day utilization is genuinely monotone non-decreasing within a reset window. INFERRED from the observed 29->33->52->59->74->83->85->87->90 sequence plus the semantics of a cumulative fraction, but not confirmed from vendor documentation. Three recommendations (lower-bound estimator, recording `rejected` as 1.0, forecast-to-budget ratio) depend on it. One explicit check across a full week's logs would settle it.

Whether utilization can be sampled when no session is running. Current evidence says no — the field appears only in a live session's stream-json. If so, the gauge is blind exactly during idle periods, and the forecast must extrapolate from the last in-session sample rather than observe. No non-session polling path was verified to exist.

The harness's SHARE of account-wide utilization. Never measured. Every 'returns N percentage points' estimate in the post-mortem is an upper bound until paired (delta local cost, delta account utilization) observations exist. This is the single highest-value unknown.

Whether a checkpoint/relaunch segment boundary is net-positive at any placement in this loop. Relaunch re-pays a 44,288-token preamble plus re-orientation measured at 23.9% of prompt volume; retained prefix costs grow superlinearly with turns. The crossover point is computable from existing transcripts but has not been computed. Until it is, a turn cap is a guess.

Whether Jenkins quietDown actually auto-expires via a timeout thread and QUEUES rather than drops new triggers. Both details came from secondary/KB sources (docs.cloudbees.com/d/kb-203737684 and blog posts), not from fetched jenkins.io primary documentation. Both are load-bearing for the auto-expiring-hold recommendation and should be verified against jenkins.io before implementation.

The correct effective-false-positive denominator for a pacing gate. Google's <10% floor is defined over code-review findings with a per-finding 'NOT USEFUL' signal. A pacing hold has no analogous per-event adjudication unless one is designed — i.e. the dryrun period needs a defined ground truth for 'this hold would have been correct' before the floor means anything.

Whether any published, controlled evidence exists for compaction, sub-agent delegation, or JIT retrieval in coding agents. None was located; both the pro (Anthropic) and con (Cognition) primary sources are explicitly reasoning-only. This is a genuine gap in the literature, not a gap in the search.

Whether the 6 blind security evals (14r-c-2) represent a real exploitable exposure or a testing-coverage gap only. The post-mortem labels it LIVE SECURITY EXPOSURE, but this research pass did not verify the underlying reducers. It affects whether that work qualifies for the security exemption carve-out under a cordon.

research.topic: Quality-gate stack for a Rust + TypeScript codebase written mostly by an autonomous agent (Monster Realm): cargo-mutants in practice, ratchet design, property testing, escaped-defect detection, and simplification pressure

findings.claim: cargo-mutants is installed at 27.1.0 and that IS the current latest release (crates.io max_version 27.1.0, updated 2026-06-02). The toolchain is pinned at Rust 1.96.0 with rustfmt/clippy and wasm32 target. There is no version-currency problem to solve here.
findings.source: MEASURED: `cargo mutants --version` -> `cargo-mutants 27.1.0`; `/home/mdrewt/.cargo/bin/cargo-mutants`; https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/cargo-mutants (max_version 27.1.0, updated 2026-06-02T15:18:24Z); /home/mdrewt/projects/ai-apps/claude-harness/projects/monster-realm/rust-toolchain.toml:3

findings.claim: `--in-diff <DIFF>` / `-D` EXISTS in the installed binary: "Include only mutants in code touched by this diff". So does `--iterate` (skip mutants caught in previous runs), `--shard k/n` with `--sharding round-robin|slice`, `--annotations github` (GitHub PR annotations, default `auto`), `--in-place`, `--skip-calls`, and `--error`. None of these are used by this repo today.
findings.source: MEASURED: `cargo mutants --help` on this machine (Filters section: `-D, --in-diff`, `--iterate`, `-p/--package`; Execution: `--shard`, `--sharding`; Output: `--annotations`; Build/Copying: `--in-place`). Repo usage: /home/mdrewt/projects/ai-apps/claude-harness/projects/monster-realm/justfile:72 (`cargo mutants -p game-core`) and :120 (`cargo mutants -p monster-realm-module --test-tool nextest`)

findings.claim: The cargo-mutants book documents TWO caveats on --in-diff that bound how much it can replace: (a) "it's certainly possible that edits in one region cause code in a different region or a different file to no longer be well tested"; (b) "The diff is only matched against the code under test, not the test code" — so a PR that only deletes tests generates zero mutants. And explicitly: "Incremental tests are helpful for giving faster feedback, but they're not a substitute for a full test run." --in-diff is therefore an ADDITION to the nightly, never a replacement.
findings.source: https://mutants.rs/in-diff.html
findings.caveat: Caveat (b) is load-bearing for this project specifically: 72.2% of in-window insertions are test+eval code, and a slice that guts a test file would produce an empty --in-diff run that reads green.

findings.claim: The book's own recommended CI shape is: run on push-to-main and on PRs, use `paths:` filters so non-code changes don't trigger, install via `taiki-e/install-action`, run `cargo mutants -vV --in-place`, and upload `mutants.out` as an artifact with `if: always()`. Two named strategies: "Check mutants in pull request diffs" ("typically _much_ faster than testing all mutants") and full checking on main. This repo already uses taiki-e/install-action but does NOT use `--in-place`, does NOT upload mutants.out, and runs mutation ONLY nightly with no PR leg.
findings.source: https://mutants.rs/ci.html and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sourcefrog/cargo-mutants/main/examples/workflows/basic.yml ; repo: .github/workflows/nightly.yml (jobs `mutation`, `mutation-server`; no artifact upload, no `--in-place`); .github/workflows/ci.yml (no mutation step at all)

findings.claim: CORRECTION to the brief: ADR-0183 does NOT record ~155 min hosted. It records 26 min LOCAL for 753 mutants and leaves the hosted duration cell empty ("—"). The only recorded hosted runtime in the corpus is 43 min at the 499-mutant scale (2026-07-15). Naive scaling puts 753 mutants at roughly 60-70 hosted minutes. A grep for "155" across all 162 ADRs returns nothing.
findings.source: MEASURED: docs/adr/0183-nightly-mutation-gate-rebaseline-and-failure-visibility.md:40-42 (local head 753/323/379/51, 26 min; local baseline 513/299/181/33, 13 min; hosted row duration = "—"); docs/adr/0050-*.md:202-206 ("Re-baseline check 2026-07-15: 43 min observed on the hosted runner at the 499-mutant scale"); `grep -rn "155" docs/adr/` -> no match

findings.claim: cargo-mutants has NO built-in mutation-score / survivor-ratio threshold. There is no `--min-score`, `--threshold` or equivalent anywhere in `--help`, and ADR-0050 states this in prose. Any rate-based ratchet must be computed by the caller from `mutants.out`. The machine-readable input for that already exists: `mutants.out/outcomes.json` "describing the results of all tests, summary counts of each outcome, and the cargo-mutants version", alongside caught.txt / missed.txt / timeout.txt / unviable.txt / mutants.json.
findings.source: MEASURED: full `cargo mutants --help` output (no threshold option in any section); docs/adr/0050-*.md:192 ("cargo-mutants has no built-in survivor-count cap"); https://mutants.rs/mutants-out.html
findings.caveat: The justfile ratchet currently parses missed.txt with `grep -c ''` (justfile:138). outcomes.json gives caught+missed+unviable+timeout in one structured read, which is what a RATE needs — missed.txt alone cannot produce a denominator.

findings.claim: Handling equivalent mutants WITHOUT touching production source is already solved here and already done correctly. `.cargo/mutants.toml` uses `exclude_re` with three line-pinned, individually-justified entries, and a fourth was RETIRED when it stopped being equivalent. The book's guidance is: attribute (`#[mutants::skip]`) for individual hard-to-test functions so the skip is visible in code; config-file path/regex filter when a whole module is untestable. Config keys are `exclude_re`, `examine_re`, `exclude_globs`, `examine_globs`, `skip_calls`; CLI equivalents `-E/--exclude-re`, `-F/--re`, `-e/--exclude`, `-f/--file`. Since 27.0.0 CLI filters COMBINE with config filters rather than replacing them.
findings.source: MEASURED: /home/mdrewt/.../monster-realm/.cargo/mutants.toml (3 entries + a documented retirement, each with a proof of equivalence and a line-pin rationale); https://mutants.rs/skip.html; https://mutants.rs/filter_mutants.html
findings.caveat: NOT_APPLICABLE as a CHANGE: there is nothing to fix. The `concat!()` production-source pollution (server-module/src/accounts.rs:54, server-module/src/pvp.rs:63) is NOT caused by cargo-mutants — it is a dodge for the hand-rolled eval scanners. Do not conflate the two problems.

findings.claim: The absolute survivor cap is calibrated finer than the tool's own reproducibility. ADR-0183 D1/D2 record that the SAME semantic tree measures 323 missed locally and 324 hosted — a one-mutant environment sensitivity — and the ADR chose 324 explicitly because "the gate executes on the hosted runner". A cap of 324 therefore has an error bar of +/-1 that it cannot distinguish from a real regression. Expressed as a RATE the same delta is 42.90% vs 43.03% survival — inside any sane rate tolerance.
findings.source: MEASURED: docs/adr/0183-*.md:40-42, :54-59 ("exactly one hosted-only" survivor; unviable 51 local / 52 hosted), :64-73 (D2, "The cap is 324, not 323")

findings.claim: Rate-based mutation gating is the mainstream prior art and both major ecosystems ship it natively. StrykerJS exposes `thresholds: { high: 80, low: 60, break: null }` on the mutation SCORE (a percentage) — `break` is the build-failing one, and it is null by default so the score is advisory until you opt in. Stryker also ships `incremental: false` / `incrementalFile: "reports/stryker-incremental.json"` for cached cross-run results.
findings.source: https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-js/configuration/
findings.caveat: No Rust equivalent exists as a flag; you get the concept, not the implementation. cargo-mutants must be wrapped.

findings.claim: Infection (PHP) is the closest complete precedent for the exact gate shape this project needs: `--min-msi` and `--min-covered-msi` are RATE thresholds (Mutation Score Indicator, percent), and `--git-diff-filter` (`AM`/`A`), `--git-diff-base` (e.g. `origin/$GITHUB_BASE_REF`) and `--git-diff-lines` restrict mutation to the PR. The docs say the diff filters are "Best to be used during pull request builds on CI" and that line-level filtering "can significantly improve performance since fewer Mutants are generated". `--logger-github` emits GitHub annotations for escaped mutants. That is exactly `cargo mutants --in-diff` + `--annotations github` + a rate computed from outcomes.json.
findings.source: https://infection.github.io/guide/command-line-options.html

findings.claim: Betterer is the canonical ratchet tool and its key property is the one this project lacks: `betterer ci` fails if the new result differs from the committed `.betterer.results` in EITHER direction. Getting worse fails. Getting BETTER also fails, because it proves the committed baseline no longer reflects reality and must be updated in the same diff. That two-way check is precisely what prevents "re-baseline == quiet loosening".
findings.source: https://phenomnomnominal.github.io/betterer/docs/running-betterer/ (and https://charpeni.com/blog/enforce-best-practices-incrementally-with-betterer)

findings.claim: This repo has ALREADY independently reinvented the Betterer ratchet, correctly, in one place — and it is the best gate in the corpus. `evals/scanner-migration-audit.eval.mjs` holds `KNOWN_UNMIGRATED_CAP = 7` ("EXACTLY the number of KNOWN_UNMIGRATED entries below, so the debt list can only ever shrink: adding an eleventh park requires editing this constant in the same diff, in the open") plus per-entry validation that each parked file must EXIST, be in the gated set, and STILL FAIL — "the moment a later slice migrates one, this gate REDs demanding the entry be deleted". Each entry carries an owner (`14r-c-2`) and a MEASURED reason. Named debt with a monotone-shrinking allowlist beats a scalar cap on every axis: it survives growth, it cannot be re-baselined silently, and it names who owns each item.
findings.source: MEASURED: evals/scanner-migration-audit.eval.mjs:121-124 (cap constant + rationale), :126-134 (self-retiring validation), :135-160 (KNOWN_UNMIGRATED entries with owner + measured canary reason)
findings.caveat: This is the format to GENERALISE (per the standing rule about generalising what works). It is currently applied to exactly one problem.

findings.claim: Per-diff coverage (diff-cover / Codacy / Codecov patch coverage) is the coverage-world answer to baseline drift: "if you touch a line of code, that line should be covered" — the gate is a property of the diff, so a growing codebase cannot dilute it and there is no baseline to re-negotiate. It composes with, and does not replace, an absolute floor.
findings.source: https://pypi.org/project/diff-cover/ ; https://blog.codacy.com/diff-coverage
findings.caveat: The repo's vitest coverage gate is nightly-only (`just coverage`, .github/workflows/nightly.yml `coverage` job) and there is no lcov/cobertura emission wired for a diff-cover-style tool today.

findings.claim: Property-based testing is NOT the gap — it is already broadly adopted on both sides. Rust: `proptest` is a workspace dependency and a game-core dev-dependency, with 34 `proptest!` macro sites across 28 files including combat/resolve.rs, combat/status.rs, combat/weather.rs, trading/rules.rs, currency.rs, ranking.rs, evolution gating and taming. TypeScript: `fast-check` ^3.21.0 is a devDependency with 113 `fc.assert` call sites across ~40 client test files (battleModel, tradeModel, shopModel, predictor, interpolation, reconnectPolicy, ...). Any recommendation to "introduce property testing" would be re-proposing something already done.
findings.source: MEASURED: Cargo.toml workspace.dependencies `proptest = "1"`; game-core/Cargo.toml [dev-dependencies]; `grep -rn "proptest!" --include=*.rs | wc -l` = 34 across 28 files; client/package.json devDependencies `fast-check: ^3.21.0`; `grep -rn "fc.assert" client evals | wc -l` = 113

findings.claim: Current library versions for reference: proptest max 1.11.0 (repo tracks `"1"`, so it floats and is current); fast-check latest 4.9.0 while the repo pins `^3.21.0` — one major version behind, and `^3` will never take it. fast-check v4 is a deliberate migration, not a drift fix.
findings.source: MEASURED: https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/proptest (max_version 1.11.0); https://registry.npmjs.org/fast-check/latest (4.9.0); client/package.json
findings.caveat: Low priority. A major-version bump of the property library is exactly the kind of work that consumes credits without closing an escaped-defect class.

findings.claim: There is genuinely NO reducer-executing test harness available to buy or import. The dependency tree contains spacetimedb 2.6.1 / 1.12.0, spacetimedb-bindings-macro, spacetimedb-bindings-sys, spacetimedb-lib, spacetimedb-primitives, spacetimedb-query-builder, spacetimedb-sats — and no `spacetimedb-testing` or equivalent. `bindings-sys` is the wasm host-ABI shim, so a reducer body cannot execute natively at all. A code search of clockworklabs/SpacetimeDB surfaces only the project's own internal TESTING.md and bench crate, not a published module-test crate. The only executing path is publish-then-call, which this repo already has (nightly `smoke-republish` job, and the `e2e` job with a pinned 2.6.0 CLI).

findings.claim: The structural fix for "a security guard removable without any test failing" already has a proven in-repo template, and it does not need any new tooling. `game-core/src/trading/rules.rs` exposes pure `check_headroom(...)` (:404) and `authorize_respond` / `authorize_confirm` (:444, :459); the server-module reducer is a thin adapter that calls them. Those pure seams carry 13+ real behavioural tests in-crate. The same shape is `evaluate_train`/`evaluate_care` behind raising_tests.rs (54 tests, 1 source-read) and `evaluate_condition` in dialogue/rules.rs:44. Once a guard lives in game-core, cargo-mutants' zero-tolerance `mutate-core` gate covers it automatically — deleting the guard IS a mutant, and it must be killed. The source-scan then only has to prove the reducer still CALLS the seam, which is a one-line, robust needle rather than a whole-file semantic scan.

findings.claim: THE SINGLE LARGEST UNCLAIMED WIN: the correct observability check ALREADY EXISTS, is well written, and has ZERO mechanical callers. `ops/observability/validate.mjs` runs `docker compose config --quiet` with rendered env, then each config through ITS OWN upstream validator inside the exact pinned image — `promtool check config`, `promtool check rules`, `alloy fmt`, `loki -verify-config`, `tempo -config.verify`, `caddy validate` (against the BUILT image, which is the only thing that proves the caddy-ratelimit plugin is compiled in). It reports `skipped` loudly when docker is absent and never silently passes. A repo-wide grep for `validate.mjs` returns only the file itself, README prose, and an ARCHITECTURE.md sentence claiming "8/8 tier-2 validators" — a one-time hand-run result recorded as if it were a gate. It is in no justfile recipe, no workflow, and no eval.
findings.source: MEASURED: ops/observability/validate.mjs:1-206 (esp. :127 `docker compose config --quiet`, :129-155 in-image validators, :160-196 caddy build+validate, :115-121 explicit skip-is-not-a-pass); `grep -rn "validate\.mjs" .` -> ARCHITECTURE.md:1405, ops/observability/README.md:52,117,122, and the file itself. No justfile / no .github / no evals hit.

findings.claim: Neither compose file defines a single `healthcheck:`, and every service carries `restart: unless-stopped`. That combination is why 4 of 8 containers crash-looped through a CLEAN merge: `docker compose up -d` returns success, `docker compose ps` shows containers, and the restart policy keeps resurrecting the dead ones. `docker compose up --wait` ("Wait for services to be running|healthy. Implies detached mode") plus `--wait-timeout` is the cheap continuous check — but with zero healthchecks it can only wait for "running", which a crash-looper transiently satisfies. Healthchecks are the prerequisite, not an optional nicety.
findings.source: MEASURED: `grep -c healthcheck ops/observability/docker-compose.yml ops/auth/docker-compose.yml` -> 0 and 0; `restart: unless-stopped` on all 8 services in ops/observability/docker-compose.yml; https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/up/
findings.caveat: Every service already exposes a natural probe target on loopback: prometheus 9090, alloy 12345, grafana 3001/api/health, node_exporter 9100, mr-trace-relay 9101/health, caddy, plus loki/tempo. A `healthcheck:` per service is ~8 small diffs and is the enabling change for --wait.

findings.claim: The repo contains a live, documented instance of the exact pathology the post-mortem names: production configuration deliberately shaped to satisfy broken test infrastructure. tempo's `-server.http-listen-address=127.0.0.1` "DOES NOT EXIST in tempo 2.10.7 (nor 3.0.2): `flag provided but not defined`, and the container dies on start. It is retained only because deleting it reds `checkListenAddrsLoopback`". The comment goes on to admit "that predicate's tempo pass is EVIDENCE-FREE". A committed config knowingly kept broken so a text scanner stays green is the config-layer twin of the `concat!()` dodge in accounts.rs:54 / pvp.rs:63.
findings.source: MEASURED: ops/observability/docker-compose.yml, tempo service `command:` block comment ("PARKED, ADR-0190 D1"); evals/observability-stack-config.eval.mjs:153-157 (the prescribed repair, including "Proof: `docker compose up -d tempo` reaches a non-restarting state"); server-module/src/accounts.rs:54; server-module/src/pvp.rs:63

findings.claim: The eval layer already KNOWS the structured-tool answer and declined it as out of scope — twice, in writing. The red-team file records that a quoted service key hid an entire rogue service from four gates "while `docker compose config --services` listed all 8; the scanner saw 7", and the eval says "the durable fix is gating `docker compose config` output, which is out of scope". So a hand-written YAML-ish text parser (46,432 lines of predicate module + 65,522 lines of its test file + 11,165 of red-team regressions) exists to re-derive what one 30ms subprocess call already returns correctly.
